Investigations/SOC-03

Invoice fraud phishing analysis

Triage of a suspected invoice-fraud email: headers, authentication, sender identity, links, attachment and response.

Training exerciseEmail analysis

01

Project introduction

An email claiming to be from the supplier MedEquip Solutions reached the Accounts Payable mailbox of MediSure Health Network on Monday 9 September 2024 at 07:14 UTC. It said Invoice #MSH-2024-0912 was past due and demanded $18,740.00 within 24 hours, with a threat to halt medical supply delivery.

The message was examined as a SOC case-study exercise and classified as malicious invoice fraud (business email compromise).

Training sampleThe domains, addresses and hash are fabricated indicators. Reputation lookups such as MXToolbox, VirusTotal and AbuseIPDB were deliberately not used, because they do not apply to made-up indicators.

03

Header and authentication analysis

The only Received header names mail.medequip-invoices.com at 192.168.0.50, a private (RFC 1918) address. A legitimate internet sender cannot present a private address to a public mail server, which points to an incomplete or falsified header chain. With a single hop there is no relay path to follow and no IP reputation to check.

CheckResultMeaning
SPFfailThe sending IP is not authorised for medequip-invoices.com, and that domain differs from the visible From domain, so it would not align even on a pass.
DKIMnoneThe message is unsigned, so origin and integrity cannot be verified.
DMARCfail, action=quarantineThe visible From domain failed authentication and alignment, and the published policy calls for quarantine.

Analogy: SPF is the guest list at the door, DKIM is the signature on a letter, and DMARC is the host's instruction for what to do when either check fails.

LimitationThe headers record the DMARC disposition but do not show what the gateway actually did with the message, so the message trace should be checked to confirm it was held.

04

Sender identity

HeaderValue
Frombilling@medequip-solutions.com, the vendor identity shown to the reader
Return-Path / Message-IDmedequip-invoices.com, the lookalike domain that actually sent it
Reply-ToA free-mail address that diverts replies away from the vendor domain

The X-Mailer header shows PHPMailer 6.1.2, a general-purpose PHP mailing library often used by bulk and phishing mailers, rather than a billing system. The message is flagged X-Priority 1 to add urgency, and the Message-ID contains the string acctrecovery, echoing the Reply-To address.

05

Links, tracking pixel and attachment

  • ConfirmedLink mismatch. The HTML Review & Pay Invoice button and the plain-text link point to two unrelated registrable domains. Both put the vendor name in a subdomain to look familiar.
  • ConfirmedTracking pixel. A hidden 1x1 image loaded over plain HTTP reports when the email is opened, telling the sender the mailbox is active.
  • ConfirmedDisguised attachment. The body promises a PDF, but the file is Invoice_MSH-2024-0912.html containing only a script block. This matches the HTML-smuggling pattern. In this sample the script is a placeholder with no executable content.
06

Timestamp analysis

The Date header (07:14:50) and the receipt time (07:14:52) are in the correct order, so the header timestamps show no anomaly. The content is less consistent: it says accounts more than 30 days past due face suspension, yet the invoice was due on 7 September 2024, only two days before the email arrived.

07

Justification

This is an attempt at fraudulent vendor invoice spoofing. The basis is a private originating IP, a lookalike sending domain, SPF, DKIM and DMARC failures, a free-mail Reply-To, two distinct credential-harvesting links, a tracking pixel, an HTML attachment shown as a PDF, scripted mailer tooling, an overdue claim that contradicts its own dates, urgency, and threats aimed at a healthcare supply chain.

09

Recommendations

  • InterpretationPayment controls. Verify urgent invoices and bank-detail changes by phone using contact details already on file, and require dual approval.
  • InterpretationEmail security. Apply SPF, DKIM and DMARC results consistently, enable impersonation protection for key vendor domains, tag external senders and flag Reply-To mismatches.
  • InterpretationAttachments and links. Block or sandbox external HTML attachments, enable time-of-click URL scanning and block remote images by default.
  • InterpretationTraining. Invoice-fraud awareness and phishing simulations for finance and procurement staff.
  • InterpretationResponse. Block the indicators, search mailboxes for related messages and remove them, review proxy and DNS logs, reset credentials for anyone who entered them, and notify MedEquip.
10

Limitations

  • LimitationTraining sample. Indicators are fabricated, so no reputation or threat-intelligence checks were possible.
  • LimitationSingle hop. No relay path exists to trace.
  • LimitationGateway action unconfirmed. The message trace is needed to confirm quarantine.
11

Skills demonstrated

Email header analysisSPF, DKIM and DMARC interpretationPhishing triageMIME and attachment inspectionIOC extraction and defangingBusiness email compromise recognitionResponse recommendations
12

Final takeaway

Authentication results should have stopped this message, but the headers alone do not prove they did.

Attackers register new lookalike domains cheaply, which is why payment verification, impersonation protection and finance-focused training are needed alongside SPF, DKIM and DMARC.
